value.overview: The Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) is a distinctive coastal waterbird known for its unusually shaped bill, in which the lower mandible extends beyond the upper. It flies low over calm water with its bill partly open, using the lower mandible to detect and catch small fish. Black Skimmers are social and often gather in flocks on beaches, sandbars, estuaries, lagoons, and other open shores. They are members of the gull and tern family, Laridae.
value.classification: The Black Skimmer belongs to the order Charadriiformes and family Laridae. It is the only skimmer species found in the Americas and is currently recognized as Rynchops niger.
value.identification: Adults have a black crown, back, and upper wings contrasting with white cheeks, underparts, and wing markings. The long, laterally compressed bill is red near the base and black toward the tip, with the lower mandible noticeably longer than the upper. Legs are short and reddish. Juveniles are browner and more mottled above. The distinctive bill, low flight over water, and graceful flocking behavior make this species difficult to confuse with other Costa Rican shorebirds.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black Skimmer occurs widely along the coasts and major waterways of the Americas. It uses beaches, sandbars, mudflats, estuaries, lagoons, tidal creeks, coastal marshes, and shallow bays, usually where open, sparsely vegetated resting or nesting sites are available. In Costa Rica it is a coastal visitor recorded along both the Pacific and Caribbean regions, including estuaries and river mouths such as the Tárcoles area. It is not generally associated with forested or upland habitats.
value.migrationStatus: Costa Rica is used mainly outside the breeding season. Northern populations move south into tropical waters, while some South American birds move north and may reach Costa Rica. The species is therefore an uncommon or locally regular nonbreeding visitor in suitable coastal habitats, rather than a known regular breeder there.
value.breeding: Black Skimmers usually breed colonially on open sandy beaches, shell banks, gravel bars, dredge-spoil islands, and sparsely vegetated coastal islands. The nest is a shallow scrape on bare or lightly covered ground. Both adults incubate the eggs and defend the colony, often near terns or other colonial waterbirds. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching but remain dependent on adults for food. Reliable sources do not indicate an established regular breeding population in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: Small fish make up most of the diet, with crustaceans and other small aquatic animals also taken. The skimmer flies with its lower mandible slicing through the surface of calm, shallow water. When the bill contacts prey, the jaws close rapidly. Feeding may occur during daylight or at night, especially when water conditions are calm and prey are concentrated near the surface. Individuals also pick food from the water or mud when conditions are unsuitable for skimming.
value.behavior: Black Skimmers are highly social and commonly rest or travel in flocks ranging from a few birds to many dozens. They are strongest and most graceful in flight, often circling, banking, and landing together. Outside breeding colonies they are generally quiet, but they give barking or yapping calls when disturbed or interacting with flock members. They spend much of the day resting on sandbars, beaches, mudflats, or low islands near feeding areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not fully quantified, but available evidence indicates an overall decline or suspected decline, with stronger decreases documented in several North American breeding populations.
conservation.threats: Important threats include loss and degradation of beaches, sandbars, estuaries, and other open coastal habitats; disturbance by people, vehicles, boats, and dogs; predation at nesting colonies; coastal development; pollution; and changing water levels or storm patterns. Because the species nests on open ground, eggs and chicks are especially vulnerable to trampling and disturbance. In Costa Rica, protection of quiet estuaries, beaches, river mouths, and sandbars is particularly relevant for visiting birds.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect coastal wetlands, beaches, sandbars, and estuaries from unnecessary development and disturbance. Keep dogs and vehicles away from resting or nesting flocks, observe colonies from a distance, and follow local closures or wildlife-area guidance. Support wetland conservation and responsible coastal tourism, reduce plastic and other pollution, and report sightings through established bird-monitoring programs so seasonal use of Costa Rican sites can be better documented.
